meta.title: Who really said "It Took Me Fifteen Years to Discover That I Had No Talent for Writing. Did You Quit?"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Groucho Marx. The joke ran unsigned in Puck in February 1912 — about poetry, over ten years — and "Did you quit?" is a 2012 research headline.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'It Took Me Fifteen Years to Discover That I Had No Talent for Writing. Did You Quit?'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Groucho. An unsigned 1912 Puck joke, credited to Twain in 1946 and Benchley in 1949 — four years after Benchley had died.

answer.label: Not Groucho Marx — an anonymous 1912 magazine joke
answer.authorDates: Unsigned dialogue printed 28 February 1912 · probably later used by Robert Benchley, 1889–1945
answer.sourceLine: Groucho Marx has no documented claim on this line at all. The joke was already in print as an unsigned dialogue in the humour magazine Puck on 28 February 1912 — about failing at poetry, over “nearly ten years,” not fifteen. It was pinned on Mark Twain in 1946 and on Robert Benchley in 1949, and the snappy second line — “Did you quit?” — appears in no period source at all: it is the headline Quote Investigator ↗ wrote over its own 2012 investigation.

source.heading: The 1912 original — about poetry, and ten years

docMeta.dd: Puck, vol. 71 (28 February 1912), p. 5, col. 3 — "Couldn't Afford To Then"
Unsigned. Speakers are generic: SCRIBBLER and FRIEND
Walter Winchell's column, 26 January 1946 — still "ten years"
Reader's Digest 55 (September 1949), p. 118 — first appearance of "15 years"

source.excerpt:
SCRIBBLER.—It took me nearly ten years to learn that I couldn’t write poetry.
FRIEND.—Gave it up then, did you?
SCRIBBLER.—Oh, no. By that time I had a reputation.
trail: The earliest printing is the unsigned dialogue “Couldn’t Afford To Then” in Puck, 28 February 1912, reprinted with credit to Puck in three newspapers the following month — located and transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗, which cites the volume to HathiTrust.

That volume is checkable: Penn Libraries’ Online Books Page listing for Puck ↗ states that volumes “1-3, 5-7, 9-34, 37-38, 49-50, 52, 55, 58, 62, 65, 71-72, 75-77, and 80-81” of the English edition are freely viewable — volume 71 among them.

The Benchley credit rests on one late, second-hand source. Wikiquote ↗ cites only Nathaniel Benchley’s Robert Benchley (1955), ch. 1 — a book McGraw-Hill published in 1955 ↗, ten years after Robert Benchley’s death.

The Groucho credit has no foothold anywhere: the line appears nowhere on his Wikiquote page ↗, which does maintain a Misattributed section — so its absence there is meaningful rather than an accident of how that page is organised.
source.excerptNote: Note what is not here: no fifteen years, no “no talent for writing,” no “too famous,” and no Groucho, Twain or Benchley. The subject is poetry. Those elements accumulated over the following decades, and the wording quoted today — transcribed in Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗ — is first recorded in 1949.
source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted for the wording on this page. The 1912 Puck ancestor is long out of copyright, but that is not the sentence people quote. The familiar “fifteen years… too famous” wording is first documented in Reader’s Digest in September 1949 and in Nathaniel Benchley’s 1955 McGraw-Hill biography ↗ — both well after 1931 — with no identifiable author behind the phrasing itself, and the paired second line is a 2012 editorial headline. Treat it as of uncertain status rather than assuming it is free to reuse.

author.name: Robert Benchley
author.kicker: The humorist whose name it landed on
author.heading: Robert Benchley — the man who probably used it, and certainly didn't write it
author.metaLine: 1889–1945 · American humorist, drama critic and actor
author.bio: Robert Charles Benchley (1889–1945) was an American humorist, drama critic and actor, a founding member of the Algonquin Round Table who wrote for Vanity Fair, Life and The New Yorker before a second career in short comic films. His speciality was the flustered ordinary man defeated by ordinary things, delivered in a tone of unbothered self-deprecation — which is exactly why this joke fits him so comfortably, and exactly why it stuck to him. He did not invent it. Quote Investigator finds the gag in print in 1912, when Benchley was twenty-two and years from publishing humour, and his name was first attached to it in Reader’s Digest in September 1949, four years after his death.

copyAttribution: Not Groucho Marx. The joke first appeared as an unsigned dialogue in Puck, vol. 71 (28 February 1912), p. 5, under the title "Couldn't Afford To Then" — and it was about poetry, over "nearly ten years," not fifteen. Walter Winchell credited it to Mark Twain in January 1946; Reader's Digest credited it to Robert Benchley in September 1949, four years after Benchley's death. The second line, "Did you quit?", is the headline of Quote Investigator's 2012 article, not wording from any period source. — Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: Three names, none of them the author
misattribution.intro: This is an unusually well-documented case of a joke acquiring famous owners it never had. Quote Investigator’s chronology shows the gag in print, unsigned, decades before any of the three men now credited with it were named — and shows that the two-line form circulating today was assembled by a modern researcher, not by anyone in the period.

items.scope: The credit this page was asked about
items.why: Groucho appears exactly once in the documented record of this joke, and not as its speaker: in Charlotte Chandler’s 1978 interview book he recalls Benchley saying a related but different line — “I realized I wasn’t funny, but I’d been doing it for fifteen years, and I was so successful I couldn’t stop” (Quote Investigator ↗). The line is absent from his Wikiquote page ↗ entirely, including the Misattributed section that page maintains.

Walter Winchell’s syndicated column of 26 January 1946, under the heading “Little Known Stories About Well-Known People,” is the earliest known Twain attribution — thirty-six years after Twain’s death, and Winchell’s version still says ten years. The 1972 collection Everyone’s Mark Twain repeats it, but its own supporting citation is a 1952 newsletter (Quote Investigator ↗).

Reader’s Digest’s “Quotable Quotes” column of September 1949 is the first known Benchley credit and the first appearance of “15 years.” Benchley died in November 1945. His son Nathaniel repeated it as something his father “once said” in his 1955 biography, which is the sole citation Wikiquote ↗ offers. Quote Investigator’s verdict is careful and worth preserving: Benchley probably used the joke, but did not create it.

No period source contains these words. They are the title Quote Investigator gave its own article. The actual recorded responses are “Gave it up then, did you?” (1912), “I suppose you gave it up, then?” (1912 and 1920), “You gave up?” (1936) and “And you gave it up?” (Winchell, 1946) — all transcribed in the investigation itself ↗. Any page presenting “Did you quit?” as a historical quotation is quoting the researcher, not the record.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer: an anonymous gagwriter for Puck, in February 1912, wrote a joke about giving up on poetry — and it has been finding famous mouths to live in ever since (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: A joke with a thirty-seven-year head start on its author
lead: Most misattributions are a famous name stealing a line from an obscure one. This is stranger: the line never had an author to steal from. It surfaces in Puck in February 1912 as filler — a two-line exchange between characters called SCRIBBLER and FRIEND, unsigned, sold by the column-inch. Within weeks it had been clipped and reprinted, with credit to Puck, in the Springfield Republican, the Seattle Daily Times and the Jersey Journal. That is how jokes moved in 1912, and nobody involved imagined anyone would ever ask who wrote one.

Then it drifted. By September 1912 the failure was at stories rather than poetry; by 1936 the punchline had hardened into “by that time I was too famous”; by 1943 Evan Esar had filed it as a dictionary definition of writer. Only once the wording was fully formed did it start attracting names — Twain in 1946, Benchley in 1949, and eventually, on the internet, Groucho Marx. A joke that circulated for decades with no author at all ended up with three.
detailsBody: 1912, Puck: “It took me nearly ten years to learn that I couldn’t write poetry.” / “Gave it up then, did you?” / “Oh, no. By that time I had a reputation.”
1912, The Independent: the same shape, but the failure is now at stories, credited to the New York American. 1920, Life: reprinted as “A Popular Author,” credited to the Kansas Brown Bull.
1936, The Literary Digest: “it took me ten years to discover that I had absolutely no talent for writing literature” — and the modern punchline arrives: “Oh, no; by that time I was too famous.”

1946, Walter Winchell: the first Mark Twain credit, still at ten years. May 1949, The Saturday Review: a Jack Markow cartoon compresses it into one speaker’s line. September 1949, Reader’s Digest: the first Benchley credit, and the first “15 years.”

1978, Charlotte Chandler: Groucho Marx, interviewed near the end of his life, quotes Benchley saying something related but distinctly different — “I realized I wasn’t funny, but I’d been doing it for fifteen years, and I was so successful I couldn’t stop.” That is the entirety of Groucho’s documented involvement: he was quoting someone else.
context.pull: The gag was in newspapers when Benchley was twenty-two. His name was attached to it four years after he died.

schema.verdictNote: Commonly misattributed to Groucho Marx. The true author is not established; no creator is asserted here. The text above is the unsigned 1912 Puck original; the alternateName wording is a later form, first documented in Reader's Digest in September 1949 — not in 1912.

sourcesVerified.claim: The earliest located version is an unsigned dialogue titled "COULDN'T AFFORD TO THEN" in Puck, 28 February 1912, between speakers SCRIBBLER and FRIEND, about writing poetry: "It took me nearly ten years to learn that I couldn't write poetry." / "Gave it up then, did you?" / "Oh, no. By that time I had a reputation." QI concludes neither Twain nor Benchley created the joke, though Benchley probably used it. Note 1 gives Puck vol. 71, 28 Feb 1912, page 5 by count, col. 3, Keppler & Schwarzmann, New York (HathiTrust).

The first known Mark Twain attribution is Walter Winchell's column of 26 January 1946 (Greensboro Record, p. 6, col. 3), reading "It took me ten years to discover that I had no talent for writing." / "And you gave it up?" / "Oh, no! By that time I was too famous!"

The first known Robert Benchley attribution is Reader's Digest, "Quotable Quotes," volume 55, September 1949, page 118, which is also the first appearance of "15 years"; Nathaniel Benchley's Robert Benchley: A Biography (McGraw-Hill, 1955), page 9, later carries the full modern wording as something his father "once said."

Groucho Marx's only appearance in the record is Charlotte Chandler's Hello, I Must Be Going (Doubleday, 1978), page 272, where Groucho quotes Benchley saying a different variant: "I realized I wasn't funny, but I'd been doing it for fifteen years, and I was so successful I couldn't stop." Groucho is listed on QI's page only as a query name.

"Did you quit?" appears only as QI's own article headline; the period responses transcribed inside the article are "Gave it up then, did you?" (1912 Puck), "I suppose you gave it up, then?" (1912 Independent and 1920 Life), "You gave up?" (1936 Literary Digest) and "And you gave it up?" (1946 Winchell).

Wikiquote's Robert Benchley page carries "It took me fifteen years to discover that I had no talent for writing, but I couldn't give it up because by that time I was too famous." under its "== Quotes ==" heading, cited only as "Quoted in Robert Benchley (1955) by Nathaniel Benchley, ch. 1". Verified from raw wikitext; the page's only two headings are Quotes and External links. It also gives Benchley's dates as 15 September 1889 – 21 November 1945 and describes him as an American humorist, critic and actor.

Wikiquote's Groucho Marx page does NOT contain this line in any section. Verified from raw wikitext: a grep for "no talent for writ", "fifteen years to discover" and "too famous" returns no matches, and the page does carry a "==Misattributed==" section, so the absence is meaningful.

The Online Books Page states that HathiTrust's freely viewable English-edition holdings of Puck comprise "issues from volumes 1-3, 5-7, 9-34, 37-38, 49-50, 52, 55, 58, 62, 65, 71-72, 75-77, and 80-81" — confirming that volume 71, containing the 28 February 1912 issue, is digitised and freely viewable.

Robert Benchley (15 September 1889 – 21 November 1945) was an American humorist, newspaper columnist and actor; a founding member of the Algonquin Round Table; wrote humour for Vanity Fair from 1914, was drama critic at Life from April 1920 through 1929, and became theatre critic at The New Yorker in 1929. His son Nathaniel Benchley published a biography of him in 1955.
Nathaniel Benchley (13 November 1915 – 14 December 1981) was the son of Robert Benchley, and "He wrote a biography of his father Robert that McGraw-Hill published in 1955."

Puck was an American humour magazine published from 1876 until 1918, founded in 1876 as a German-language publication by cartoonist Joseph Keppler and businessman Adolph Schwarzmann, with editorial offices in New York City from before 1887.
